en: A Collection of Miscellaneous Parables from Various Sutras, Volume One,
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Dàoluè;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yáoqín dynasty.
(1) The wise contemplate that wealth cannot be preserved for long, being like a house caught in a fire.

A person of keen intelligence clearly recognizes the power of the flames; before the fire reaches them, they hurriedly remove their valuables. Although the house may be consumed by the blaze, the treasures remain intact, allowing them to rebuild their residence and expand their profitable enterprises.

It is the same for the wise person who plants merit and diligently practices giving: knowing that the body is fragile and material wealth is impermanent, they encounter a field of merit and give at the proper time. This is like the man who rescued goods from the fire; he will experience happiness in future lives, just as that man was comforted by the benefit of his renewed household enterprise.

Foolish and deluded people merely know how to cherish and worry; they frantically attempt to rescue what is madly confused and rendered senseless, yet they fail to measure the power of the fire or the fierce wind that cuts off the flames, leaving earth and stone scorched together. In a mere instant, everything is swept away and utterly extinguished. Since the house cannot be saved, wealth and possessions are lost, and the person must endure hunger, cold, and the suffering of grief for the rest of their life.

The person who is stingy and miserly is likewise thus: not knowing that life and body are impermanent and cannot be preserved for even a moment, they nevertheless amass, guard, and cherish them. Yet death arrives without appointment, and one suddenly passes away; the body becomes like earth or wood, and wealth and possessions are all abandoned—just as a fool suffers in grief and loses their way.

Only those of clear wisdom are able to awaken, realizing that the body is like an illusion and wealth cannot be preserved; that all things are impermanent and only merit can be relied upon; and that by leading others out of suffering, one may achieve the Way.
2. (II) A bodhisattva practices giving without begrudging even his own body or life.

For example, in the past, King Śibi gave his own body for the sake of a pigeon; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, intentionally went there to test him, wishing to know whether he truly possessed the resolve of a bodhisattva.
Śakra spoke to Viśvakarman-deva:
"Assume the body of a pigeon; I shall become a hawk to pursue you, and you must then feign fear and enter beneath the king's armpit."

Immediately, Viśvakarman transformed himself into a pigeon, and Śakra transformed himself into a hawk; the hawk flew swiftly in pursuit of the pigeon, which flew straight into the king’s armpit, its whole body trembling with fear.
At that time, the hawk, perched upon a tree, said to the king:
"Return my pigeon to me; this is my food, not yours.
The king replied:
"I first resolved my mind desiring to rescue all sentient beings and wishing to enable them to cross over suffering.
The hawk said, "The King intends to deliver all sentient beings; I too am counted among those sentient beings. Why do you alone show me no compassion and snatch away my food?"
The king replied,
"What food do you require?
The hawk said:
"I make this vow: I shall eat the fresh flesh and blood of slaughtered animals.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I make this vow: whenever any sentient beings come to take refuge in me, I shall protect them with a single mind so that they do not encounter calamity."
"What food do you require?
I shall provide it for you," said the hawk.
"What I eat is the fresh blood and flesh of those recently slaughtered.
The king then thought to himself:
"This too is difficult to obtain; unless one kills living beings, there is no way to get it. How can I kill one to give to another?"
Having thus resolved, he concentrated his mind and called someone to him, saying:
"Bring a knife and cut flesh from my thigh to give to the hawk.
The hawk then spoke to the king, saying:
"Give me only the meat, and I shall use reason to ensure that the weight of the meat is exactly equal to that of the pigeon; do not deceive me.
The king said, "Bring a scale and weigh the meat against the pigeon."

The dove’s body became increasingly heavy while the king’s flesh became increasingly light; though the king had his two thighs cut away until they were gone, they remained too light and insufficient. He then cut the two hips, the two breasts, and the flesh of the chest and back until the meat of his entire body was exhausted, yet the dove’s body was still heavy.
At that moment, as the King raised his entire body to ascend [the scale], he was at the same weight as the pigeon.
The hawk said to the King, "Great King, this matter is difficult to accomplish; why do you act thus? Return the pigeon to me."
The king said:
"The pigeon has come to take refuge with me; I shall never give it to you.

In the past and present, I have lost my body many times, yet I never cherished it for the sake of the Dharma. Now that I seek to become a Buddha, I shall surely summon my supreme resolve and remain free from regret."
All the devas, nāgas, spirits, and all the people together praised him, saying:
"For the sake of a single pigeon, the bitter anguish is such as this; this matter is truly rare.
The earth shook violently, and Viśvakarman praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
"The Great Being is truly not false; he is now the field of merit for all sentient beings.
Śakra and Viśvakarman restored him to his celestial body, and immediately caused the king's body to return to its former state.
If one seeks the Way in this manner, one may attain Buddhahood.

(3) Once upon a time, there was a man who, having been sent on a distant journey, stayed alone overnight in an empty house. At midnight, a ghost arrived carrying a dead person and placed it before him. Then another ghost came chasing after, angrily scolding the first ghost:
"This dead person belongs to me; why have you carried him here?"
The two ghosts each seized one hand and disputed over it.
The first ghost said, "There is a person here who can be questioned; who brought this dead man?
The man thought to himself:
"These two spirits possess great power; whether I speak the truth or speak falsely, I shall die. Since I cannot escape death in either case, why should I speak falsely?"
The man said, "The ghost in front brought it here.

The ghost behind became greatly enraged; he seized the hand, pulled it out, and placed it on the ground. The ghost in front then took an arm from the corpse and replaced it, and it immediately adhered.

Thus, both legs, head, and flanks were all pulled out; the corpse of a dead man was placed back in its original position, and then the two demons together ate the human body they had exchanged, wiped their mouths, and departed.
The man reflected:
"My parents gave birth to this body of mine, yet my eyes have seen two ghosts devour it entirely. Now, this body of mine consists entirely of the flesh of others; do I truly possess a body at all?"
"Is it that I have no body?
If it exists, it must all be another's body; if it does not exist, then my present body is just like this.
Having reflected thus, his mind became bewildered and distressed, like that of a madman.

At dawn the next morning, he followed the road and arrived at the neighboring country; seeing there a Buddhist stūpa and a community of monks, he did not inquire about other matters, but asked only whether his own body existed or did not exist.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Who are you? He replied:
"Nor did he even know whether this being was human or non-human?
He then related the aforementioned events in detail to the assembly of monks.
The bhikṣus said:
"This person knows for himself that there is no self; he can easily be delivered.
Then he said to him:
"Your body has been devoid of self from the very beginning; it is not only the case now!"
"However, it is merely because these four great elements combine that one reckons them as 'my body.
He was immediately ordained into the Way; by severing all afflictions, he attained the path of an Arhat.
This is what is meant by being able to reckon that the self is empty and non-existent; thus, attaining the Way is not far off.
4. (Four) One who upholds the precepts shall not fail to attain anything; one who breaks the precepts loses everything.
It is like a person who constantly makes offerings to a deity; though that person is poor and begs from all quarters, they offer worship for twelve years in search of wealth and honor.
Once the people’s hearts were thus resolved, Heaven took pity on them and manifested its own form, asking them:
"What do you seek? They replied:
"We seek wealth and honor, desiring that everything our hearts wish for be obtained."
The deity gave him a vessel called the "Vase of Virtue" (guṇakumbha) and said to him:
"Whatever you wish for shall all emerge from this vase.

By means of this, the man obtained everything his heart desired; having attained his wishes, he constructed a magnificent house and provided himself with elephants, horses, and carriages. Endowed with the seven treasures, he supplied his guests with all necessities, lacking nothing in any matter.
A guest asked him, saying, "Previously you were poor; how have you come to be so wealthy today?
He replied:
"I obtained a divine jar (*devakumbha*); from this divine jar emerge these various things, and thus my wealth is such as this.
The guest said, "Bring forth the jar so that we may see the things it produces."
He immediately brought out the jar.

From within the jar, various objects were drawn forth; the man, filled with arrogance, grasped the jar and began to dance, but holding it too loosely, he lost his grip and broke the jar, whereupon all the objects vanished instantly.

One who upholds the precepts shall obtain all manner of sublime joys, with nothing that cannot be attained; yet if a person violates the precepts, becoming arrogant and self-indulgent, they are like one who breaks a jar and loses its contents.
Therefore, those who desire the bliss of the heavens and the bliss of nirvana should firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts and never violate the precepts they have received;
for if one violates the precepts received, one will fall forever into the three miserable realms to undergo suffering, from which there will be no further time of escape.

If a person wishes to seek karmic retribution, they should constantly cultivate a virtuous mind in continuous succession without interruption; thus, at the time of death, they will be able to repel all evils and receive the fruits of their wholesome deeds.
The reason for this is that if one does not first cultivate a virtuous mind, even if one wishes to make the mind virtuous at the moment of death, it will ultimately not comply with one's intent.

It is like a king in the West who originally possessed no horses; he depleted the national treasury and searched in all four directions until he purchased five hundred horses to defend against external enemies, thereby ensuring the security of his kingdom.
Having kept the horses for a long time and finding no disturbances within the kingdom, the king reflected:
"Five hundred horses require considerable food; their maintenance is laborious and of no benefit to the affairs of state."
He then commanded his attendants to blindfold the horse and have it tread upon [the grain], so that he might eat it himself without depleting the state treasury.
Having been treading for a long time, the horse became accustomed to the circular motion.

Suddenly, a neighboring kingdom raised an army and entered the territory; the king immediately ordered the horse to be fully equipped with its trappings, and a brave general mounted it according to the rules of combat. He lashed the horse toward the enemy lines, intending to charge straight forward.
When the horses encountered the whips, they all turned around and fled, showing no intention of facing the enemy.
Seeing this, the neighboring rebels knew they were incapable of anything; they immediately pressed forward and utterly defeated the king's army.

Therefore, one should know that if those who seek wholesome karmic results wish their "horse of the mind" to remain undisturbed at the time of death, they will be able to proceed according to their wishes.

One must not fail to first train and straighten this horse of the mind; for if the horse of the mind is not first trained and straightened, when the thief of death suddenly arrives, the horse of the mind will wander aimlessly and never reach its intended destination. This is just like a king’s horse that cannot defeat the enemy and preserve his kingdom.
Therefore, one who practices wholesome thoughts must never fail to keep them constantly within their breast.
(5) When a person in poverty cuts back upon their own body and speech to offer as alms, the merit thereof is immeasurable.
For example, in the past, a king established a great assembly and made various offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
At that time, there was a poor old woman who possessed nothing at all; she constantly relied on begging to sustain her life.

Hearing that the King had invited the Buddha to hold a great assembly, he felt joy in his heart and desired to offer assistance. Reflecting upon himself, he found he possessed nothing; he had only a small amount of beans with which he wished to contribute, but his attendants would not allow him to go forward.
Thereupon, the Buddha, perceiving his virtuous mind, immediately employed his supernatural power to cause these black beans to fall everywhere into the various food vessels.
When the king saw these beans, he became enraged at the kitchen attendants and asked,
"Why have these beans been placed in the food?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"It was not the fault of the kitchen staff;
rather, it was the gift bestowed by an old, impoverished woman from outside."
"Having heard that the King had established this assembly and having no means to offer assistance, she took these few beans to contribute to the King; therefore, there are these beans in the food!
The Buddha said to the Great King, "Although the gift bestowed by this old woman was minute, the merit she gains is far greater than yours, O Great King."
The king asked,
"How is it that by providing such a variety of delicacies as offerings one gains little merit,
whereas this old woman, by giving a small amount of things in charity, instead gains much merit?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"Although Your Majesty has made various offerings, all of which were provided by the common people and thus caused no loss to you;
yet this old woman, though poor, gave whatever little beans she had to offer as assistance, and for that reason she obtained much."
"The King will receive little merit.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to the King in various ways, and both the King and his aged mother attained the fruits of the Path.

Therefore, the cultivation of merit and the planting of virtue depend solely upon a sincere heart; once one has thoroughly understood the characteristics of phenomena, what need is there to worry about the lack of results?

(6) Once there was a brahmin whose household was so impoverished that he possessed only a single cow. He would milk her once a day to obtain one *droṇa* of milk, which he used to provide for his own livelihood.

Hearing it said that by providing a meal for the assembly of monks on the fifteenth day, a śramaṇa gains great merit, he immediately stopped milking his cows. He waited until the end of the month to milk them all at once, hoping to obtain three *sheng* so that he might use them as an offering to the śramaṇas.

When the full moon arrived, he issued a great invitation to all the śramaṇas to come to his house; they all took their seats. At that time, the brāhmaṇa entered and milked a cow, obtaining exactly one *dōng* (斗); though he milked for a long time, the milk did not increase.
The people reviled and scolded him, saying: "You fool!
Why do you not milk [the cow] day after day, yet hope to obtain much even after a month has passed?"

People of the present age are also like this: when they possess wealth and goods, they are unable to practice giving according to their means; instead, they hoard them for a long time and only act when they have accumulated much. Yet impermanence, water, and fire, as well as one's own life, cannot be guaranteed for even a moment. If one does not encounter these calamities, the wealth may be squandered in a single day, leaving nothing behind. Wealth and goods endanger the person just as a venomous snake does; one must not harbor greedy attachment toward them.
For example, in the past, when the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of King Prasenajit, he saw a hidden treasure buried in the ground, filled with precious objects.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see this poisonous snake?"
Ānanda replied, "I have seen it.

At that time, there was a person walking behind the Buddha who, upon hearing these words, went to investigate. Seeing that it was indeed a fine jewel, he disparaged the Buddha’s statement as being false and flowery, saying, "This is actually a jewel, yet you call it *dhatu* (poison)."
That man immediately took this treasure privately for his family members, both great and small, and his household became immensely wealthy.
Someone reported this to the king, saying:
"This man has obtained a hidden treasure at will, yet he does not pay it to the government."
The king immediately had him arrested and interrogated regarding his treasures, which were then confiscated in full.
Yet the king remained unconvinced and subjected him to further and more diverse forms of torture; though every kind of excruciating suffering was inflicted upon him, he still did not confess.

The king was greatly incensed and wished to execute his family for seven generations; he placed him on a carriage and set out intending to kill him. The king sent someone to secretly observe what the Daoist would say, and the man immediately replied:
"The Buddha’s words are most sincere; [this snake] is truly a venomous serpent."
I did not believe it, yet now I have been bitten by a venomous snake; I know what I must say.
Had I been killed by the venomous snake, it would have affected only my own person, but now it has reached back through seven generations—truly, it is just as they said.
The messenger reported the matter in full to the king. Upon hearing these words, the king immediately summoned him back and said to the man:
"The Buddha is a person of great merit, yet you were able to remember the words he spoke to you in the past."
The king was greatly delighted and returned his treasures to him, releasing him to depart.
Because he had called to mind the Buddha’s words, he was spared from the peril of death; therefore, one must not fail to call the Buddha’s words to mind with a sincere heart.
(7) A person who upholds the precepts would rather lose their life than violate the Buddha’s teachings.

For example, in the past, there were two merchants traveling by ship at sea who wished to reach another country; they were carried along with others into the middle of the ocean when they encountered a violent wind that shattered the vessel, and the merchants seized whatever they could rely upon to save themselves.
At that time, a junior monk obtained a wooden board. The senior monk said to him:
"The Buddha taught that one should show respect to seniors; give me this board, for I do not fear violating the precepts."
Having heard these words, the junior practitioner reflected to himself:
"Which is more important?
Guarding the precepts is more important."
Having reflected thus, he thought, "I would rather die while carefully guarding the Buddha's teaching.
He then offered a wooden plank to the Elder; the junior monk immediately sank into the waters of the sea.

The water deity, seeing that this practitioner of the Way maintained the precepts in such a manner and did not violate the Buddha’s teachings, brought him to the shore; because of this practitioner’s sincere observance of the precepts, all the merchants on the boat were saved from death.
The Water Deity praised the practitioner, saying:
"You are truly a person who upholds the precepts!
Because of this testimony, it is better to uphold the precepts and die than to violate them and live.
Therefore, the virtue of the precepts can be relied upon; it is capable of rescuing one from the suffering of birth and death.
(8) All sentient beings are greedily attached to worldly pleasures and do not contemplate impermanence; they do not regard great calamities as suffering.
For example, in the past there was a man who had met with circumstances warranting death; he was bound in prison and, fearing execution, fled.

According to the laws of the kingdom, if a condemned prisoner should escape from prison, a mad elephant would be released to trample him to death. Thereupon, the mad elephant was released to pursue this criminal.

Seeing the elephant approaching, the prisoner fled and entered a dilapidated well. At the bottom of the well was a great venomous dragon with its mouth agape upward, and four poisonous snakes were at the four sides of the well. There was a single root of grass there, which the prisoner, seized by fear, grasped with one-pointed urgency. Furthermore, two white rats were gnawing at this root of grass. Above the well stood a large tree, within which was honey; throughout the day, a single drop of honey fell into the man’s mouth. Having received this single drop, he thought only of this honey and no longer remembered his various sufferings, and thus he had no further desire to leave the well.
For this reason, the Sage used it as a metaphor: "The prison is the triple world that confines sentient beings;

the mad elephant is impermanence; the well is the dwelling place of sentient beings; the venomous dragon at the bottom is hell; the four poisonous snakes are the four great elements; the grass roots are the life-root of human beings; and the white rat is the sun and moon. The sun and moon devour the life of human beings, diminishing it day by day without a moment's pause, yet sentient beings remain greedily attached to worldly pleasures and fail to contemplate these great calamities."
"Therefore, the practitioner should contemplate impermanence in order to be free from all suffering.
(9) Once there was a stingy and greedy elder whom the Buddha wished to deliver. First, he dispatched Śāriputra to preach to him on the various merits and blessings of giving.
The householder was stingy and greedy, having no intention at all to give; seeing that midday was approaching, he said to Śāriputra, "Why do you not leave?
I have no food to give you."
Śāriputra, knowing that he could not be converted, immediately returned to the Buddha’s presence.
The Buddha again dispatched Maudgalyāyana, who used his supernormal powers to convert him and preached the Dharma for him.
The elder spoke once more:
"You have performed this illusory artifice because you desire my property.
Maudgalyāyana, knowing that he could not be converted, immediately returned to the Buddha's presence.
Thereupon, the Buddha went to the house himself to break his stinginess and greed. When the elder saw that the Buddha had come in person, he paid homage to him and led him into the seat.
The Buddha, employing various skillful means to teach the Dharma, said to the elder:
"Are you able to perform the five great acts of giving?
The elder addressed the Buddha:
"I am not even able to perform a small gift, let alone a great gift!
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the five great gifts?"
The Buddha said, “Regarding the five great gifts, one must not kill living beings; are you able to do this?
The elder reflected:
"One who does not kill living beings neither uses my wealth nor causes me any loss.
He then said to the Buddha,
"I am able!"
In this sequence, he taught him up to the precept against drinking alcohol, and [the elder] replied to each, saying, "I can do it!
Thereupon, the Buddha expounded various teachings on the meaning of the five precepts for the elder:
"If one can uphold these five precepts, it is as if one has already completed the five great acts of giving.

He was immediately filled with great joy and wished to offer a single piece of coarse cotton cloth to the Buddha. He entered the storehouse to seek it, but there was nothing that was not of good quality; nevertheless, he took one piece and offered it to the Buddha.
The remaining cotton cloths in the storehouse all followed him until they reached the presence of the Buddha.
Knowing that the elder’s mind of giving was not yet settled, the Buddha said to the elder:
"When Śakra, Lord of Devas, fought with the asuras, his mind was unsettled and he was defeated three times; later, because his mind was settled, he utterly shattered the asura army."

Having heard this, the elder realized that the Buddha, the Great Sage, deeply understands the minds of men; his faith became pure, and as the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

The next day, Māra knew his thoughts and immediately transformed himself into a Buddha, intending to come and destroy him. Upon arriving at the house, because the elder had not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds, he did not recognize that it was Māra; instead, he greeted him with joy and welcome, saying, "Welcome! Please take a seat."
The Mara spoke these words to the elder:
"What I said yesterday was entirely not the word of the Buddha; you must quickly abandon it!
Having heard these words, the elder was greatly astonished.
"Though his form is that of a Buddha, what he says is not; it is like a donkey wearing a lion's skin—though its shape resembles a lion, its heart is that of a donkey.
The elder did not believe him. Māra, knowing his mind was upright, restored his body and said:
"I came specifically to test you, yet your mind cannot be turned."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Even those who have seen the Truth do not yet believe the Buddha’s words, let alone those of other paths;
this is because they have deeply investigated the underlying principle."
Therefore, a disciple of the Buddha must understand profound principles in order to be able to distinguish between the teachings of Māra and the teachings of the Buddha.
For this reason, one must study the meaning and practice generosity.
10 (Ten): A practitioner seeking the Way must not greedily become attached to beautiful forms; if one is greedy, it destroys the very root of one's merit.
For example, there was once an Arhat who frequently entered the dragon palace to eat and preached the Dharma to the dragons.
Having finished eating, he departed from the dragon palace and handed his bowl to the śrāmaṇera, instructing him to wash it. The śrāmaṇera ate the few remaining grains of rice left in the bowl;

they were exceedingly fragrant and delicious. Thereupon, the elder employed a stratagem by crawling under the teacher’s rope bed and grasping its legs with both hands. When the time arrived, he entered the dragon palace together with the rope bed.
The Dragon said,
"Since you have not yet attained the Way, why have you brought him here?
The Master replied:
"Unaware and unknowing," [he thought].
When the śrāmaṇera received the food, he further beheld the dragon girl’s upright body and incomparable, exquisite fragrance; his heart became greatly attached, and he immediately made this vow:
"I shall seize this dragon's abode and dwell in her palace."
The dragon said, "Henceforth,
do not bring this śrāmaṇera here again. After the śrāmaṇera had returned,
he practiced giving and upheld the precepts with single-minded devotion, seeking exclusively to fulfill his aspiration to quickly attain the body of a dragon.

At that time, as he circumambulated the temple, water welled up from beneath his feet; knowing for certain that he would become a nāga, he went directly to the edge of the great pond where his former teacher had entered, covered his head with his *kāṣāya*, and plunged into the water, whereupon he died.
He returned as a great dragon; because his merit was so vast, he killed that king, turning the entire pond crimson.
Before this had occurred, the teachers and the assembly of monks all reviled him, but the śrāmaṇera said:
"My mind is already resolved and the signs have already appeared."
He led the assembly of monks to the pond to see it for themselves.
For this reason, one should not be greedily attached to fine fragrances or beautiful forms; otherwise, one will lose their roots of goodness and fall into the evil realms.

11 (11) Once there was a celestial being whose merit was about to be exhausted. He knew this through seven signs: first, the flowers upon his head withered; second, the light from his neck vanished; third, his body became emaciated; fourth, sweat broke out from beneath his armpits; fifth, flies came to settle on his body; sixth, dust and dirt covered his robes; and seventh, he naturally departed from his original seat.

Knowing that his merit was exhausted and that he had descended to be born into a poor household in the human world as the offspring of a sow afflicted with scabies, he was filled with sorrow and found no joy.
Another celestial being came and asked him,
"Why are you not joyful?"
He replied, "My life is drawing to a close; I am about to be reborn below as the offspring of a sow afflicted with scabies, and that is why I am sorrowful.
That deva said:

“Śākyamuni Buddha is currently in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace preaching the Dharma for his mother; you should go there to take refuge in him and the community of bhikṣus, and you shall be able to escape from suffering.”
He then went to where the Buddha was staying and took refuge with a sincere heart; seven days later, his life came to an end.

He was reborn in the world into the family of a great elder; after his mother became pregnant, she constantly heard the sound of the Three Refuges. When the ten months were complete, he was born and fell to the ground, whereupon he knelt long and with palms joined, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
His mother was startled and, deeming it an ill omen, wished to kill him; she reflected, saying:
"The son of a householder cannot be treated so summarily; my own guilt would not be small."
He immediately went to inform the elder, explaining his thoughts in detail.

The elder said, "When people live in this world, they do not know to take refuge in the Triple Gem; yet this child was born with such knowledge, and as soon as he was born, he already knew the Triple Gem. He must be a divine being; raise him well and do not find it strange!"
"This child’s merit was such that his talent and intelligence were exceptionally outstanding, and his parents held him in great affection and esteem.
When he reached the age of five, while playing with his peers by the roadside, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana happened to pass by, and the boy went forward to pay them homage."
Śāriputra said,
"I have never seen a child pay such homage!
The boy addressed the practitioner, saying:
"Do we not know one another?

Śāriputra immediately entered meditative concentration to observe their fundamental characteristics, and thus he knew they were those devas. He then knelt upright and approached Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I pray that you, Venerable Ones, will invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come to my humble abode for a meal tomorrow."
He immediately granted his consent.
The son returned home and said to his parents, "I have just invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; I pray that the World-Honored One will deign to accept our meal tomorrow."
The parents were filled with joy and immediately provided him with the finest food and provisions from their entire wealth.
On the following day, the Buddha led the great assembly to his home; the son, along with his parents, welcomed the Buddha and paid him homage.

The Buddha immediately took his seat; water was served and the meal was finished in a short while. The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, and both the parents and their son attained the *dharmakṣānti* of the non-coming of all phenomena. Hundreds of thousands of devas and humans resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Sūtra says: "One who can exhaust [all afflictions] through loving-kindness may be described as such!
(12) Once, there was a cowherd who, while in a great marsh, saw a golden flower of exquisite beauty and radiant light. He immediately thought to himself:
"The Buddha is not far from here; I shall take this to offer him."
He immediately gathered several *hu* measures of flowers, packed them into a heavy load, and departed.

Before he had reached his destination, he was gored to death by an ox. Because his mind remained fixed on the Buddha, he was reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The palace he received was vast, magnificent, and beautiful; from its four sides grew golden lotuses upon the land, their radiance shining through all. According to the laws of the devas, as soon as one is born in heaven, one first contemplates one’s past lives and then partakes of celestial blessings.
At that time, the deva observed his own past lives and saw clearly how he had been killed by an ox while gathering flowers; filled with joy, he exclaimed:
"The Buddha’s merit and blessings are immeasurable!"
"If even one who has not yet had the opportunity to present offerings has already attained such sublime majesty, how much more so for those who constantly cultivate virtue?
Thereupon, he again took flowers from the side of the palace, along with various other articles of worship, desiring to fulfill his original vow.
When the devas saw him gathering flowers, they all went to question him:
"You have recently come to receive blessings; you ought to delight yourself with the five desires, yet why do you gather these flowers?"
The deva-son replied:

"When I was a human being, I wished to go to the Buddha to make an offering of flowers, but I did not fulfill my wish. Yet, I have still been able to be reborn here; how much more so for one who actually accomplished it! The reason I take these flowers now is that I wish to follow my original vow and increase my future merit."

At that time, all the devas gave rise to wholesome minds. Eighty-four thousand sons of gods descended together, performing celestial music and making various offerings of heavenly flowers and heavenly incense. Although they had not yet seen the Buddha within the stupas and monasteries, there were elder bhikṣus who had attained the Way preaching the Dharma for them. Hearing the Dharma, the hearts of the devas were filled with joy, their merits increased, and they were finally able to see the Buddha. With drums, music, stringed songs, and the scattering of various famous flowers, they made diverse offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks. The Buddha preached the pure and wondrous Dharma for them, and both those individuals and the eighty-four thousand devas all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

This deva and the eighty thousand devas were all his virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) in a former life; they have now inspired one another so that they have simultaneously attained the Way. (13) In the past, there was a certain great elder in a foreign land who was immensely wealthy.

He had an only son whom he cherished beyond compare. Later, the son fell ill and became gravely distressed. Despite medical treatment, he did not recover and eventually met his end. As his life was drawing to a close, he single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name. The Buddha manifested his form before him; his mind became peaceful and settled, and he was immediately reborn in heaven.

The parents, grieving for their son with deep distress, were on the verge of taking their own lives, unable to find relief. They then cremated him by fire, collected his bones, and placed them in a silver bottle. On the fifteenth day of the month, they offered food and drink of a hundred flavors before the remains, wailing aloud and rolling upon the ground in lamentation.
The Son of Heaven, observing his actions from above, thought to himself:
"If I do not manifest a transformation, he will never understand.

He immediately descended and became a young boy of eight or nine years old, tending cattle by the roadside. When the ox suddenly died and lay on the ground, the boy went to gather grass and placed it in the dead ox's mouth; he then raised his staff and struck the ox, calling out:
"Get up and eat!
Seeing what the child had done, his parents and the rest of the family laughed together and came forward to ask him,
"Whose son are you?"
"How can you be so foolish?
The ox has already died; though you place grass in its mouth, when will it ever have the chance to eat?
Yet he instead laughed and said:
"Although my ox has now died, its head and mouth still remain; yet it lifts its grass but will not eat. How much more so for your son, who has been dead for a long time!

Even if you were to burn him with fire until only a few charred bones remained on the ground, and you placed food of a hundred flavors before them while wailing and weeping, would he ever be able to eat it?"
His father’s mind was immediately opened and he asked his son, "Who are you?
The son replied:

"I am the son of an elder; having now received the Buddha's grace, I have been reborn in the heavens. Seeing that my parents were suffering from excessive grief and distress, I came to transform them.
Upon hearing this, the father’s mind was liberated; he rejoiced greatly and was no longer troubled by sorrow. Suddenly, the celestial son vanished.
Upon returning home, his parents practiced great giving, observed the precepts, recited the sutras, and cultivated the Path, thereby attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
(14) In the past, countless eons ago, there was a Buddhist monastery where more than several thousand śramaṇas resided.

He dispatched several hundred śrāmaṇeras to go on almsrounds to provide for the community of monks, requiring them to deliver one *shu* of rice daily; the Master also assigned them the task of reciting one verse each.
There was one śrāmaṇera who, as he passed through the marketplace, continued to recite the sutras while walking.
At that time, there was a worthy man in the marketplace who saw the śrāmaṇera walking and reciting;
he paid his respects and asked, "What is the practitioner reciting? He replied:
"While begging for alms to provide for the Sangha, I shall also recite one verse.
The worthy man asked again,
"If there is no other business, how many verses may you recite?"
He replied,
"I can recite more than ten verses.
He asked again:
“How many days have you been begging for alms?
He replied,
“Ninety days.”
"You shall be required to pay ninety *shu* of rice.
The worthy one said to the reciter-monk, "Simply return and recite the sutras with a peaceful mind; I shall take your place in providing the rice."
The śrāmaṇera was greatly delighted. The worthy one gave him ninety *hu* of rice; having returned to report this to his teacher, he then devoted himself to reading the sūtras.
After three months, he had mastered fourteen hundred verses and informed his teacher:
"I have finished reciting the sūtras; I must now go to the house of the donor to test my skill."
The teacher immediately granted permission.
[The student] went to the worthy one’s place and reported:
"I have received your great kindness and am able to recite the sutra in peace; now that the recitation has concluded, I have come to inform you."
The śrāmaṇera recited it with such fluency that there was no stumbling or obstruction in his phrasing.
The worthy one rejoiced and prostrated himself in homage, saying:
"May I, in future lives, be intelligent, sagacious, widely learned, and possess a retentive memory."

By virtue of this meritorious vow, in every birth throughout his successive lives, he possessed clear consciousness and a powerful memory; and when a Buddha appeared in the world, he became that Buddha’s disciple, named Ānanda, who constantly attended upon the World-Honored One and was preeminent in eloquence, penetration, and vast learning.
The Master said:

"The worthy one of that time is now Ānanda. Indeed, for those who assist in learning and whose will seeks the merit of their vows, such results are not in vain; through this karmic retribution, they obtain exactly what was wished for."

To the south of Mount Sumeru there is a great tree four thousand *li* high, upon which various *pattraka* birds dwell and roost. This tree remains constantly motionless; however, when small birds resembling quails or sparrows settle upon it, the tree immediately trembles and shakes. The *pattraka* birds say to the tree deity:
"You have no knowledge that my body is heavy, yet you do not move at first."
The small bird had not yet settled when it began to tremble again.

The tree deity said, "Although this bird is small, it has come from the bottom of the great ocean and feeds exclusively on vajras. There is no place where a vajra falls that is not destroyed; therefore, it is greatly terrified and cannot find peace."

The Sūtra provides an analogy for this: if an ordinary person understands even a single phrase of a profound sūtra and recites it with their mouth and contemplates it with their mind, the three poisons, the four māras, and the eighty thousand gates of defilement within their body can find no peace; how much more so for one who extensively gathers all dharmas to serve as a bridge for the world!
15 (15) The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You should go before the one who desires [to see me].
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I possess supernatural powers such that I can leap over Mount Sumeru; if you come from the east, I shall go west, and if you come from the north, I shall head south—how could you ever catch me?"
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Karma—both demerit and merit—is natural; it cannot be avoided.
Having flown far without ceasing, he finally fell into the mountains.

At that time, there was an old man with a cartwheel hub; as Maudgalyāyana happened to fall right before him, his appearance resembled that of a ghost. Thinking it to be some malevolent thing, the old man raised the hub and struck him, instantly breaking his body.
Maudgalyāyana was so overcome by pain that he felt deep shame and distress, causing him to completely forget his original consciousness.
The Buddha took pity on him and bestowed upon him his majestic spiritual power;
only then was Maudgalyāyana able to reflect within himself and restore his original form.
This wheelwright, the old man, was Maudgalyāyana’s father in a previous life.
While Maudgalyāyana was disputing with his father, he thought to himself:
"It would be a relief to beat this man to death and break his bones!"
It is for this reason that one incurs such calamity and retribution.
Be careful not to commit the sin of filial impiety; therefore, when living in this world, one must be prudent with both mind and speech in order to provide filial support to one’s parents.
16 (16). Once, there was a śramaṇa walking through the grass when a large snake said, "Preceptor, O practitioner of the Way.
The practitioner was startled and looked around him.
The snake said, "O practitioner!
Do not fear, do not be terrified. I pray that you will preach the sutra for me, so that I may be delivered from this sinful body."
The snake said,
"O practitioner!
Have you heard of King Ajātaśatru?"
He replied, "I have heard it.
The snake said:

"I am indeed he! The practitioner said, "King Ajātaśatru has established Buddhist stūpas and monasteries; his merit from such offerings is so lofty that he shall be reborn in the heavens. By what cause, then, have you come to this state?"
The snake said,
"When I was approaching the end of my life, a person nearby dropped a fan onto my face, which caused me to give rise to anger and led me to receive this snake body."
The practitioner then preached the sutra for him; with single-minded devotion, he listened joyfully and did not eat for seven days, after which his life ended and he was reborn in heaven.
Several months later, he offered flowers to the Buddha, which caused the multitude to marvel at him.
Standing in mid-air, he said:

"I, King Ajātaśatru, have received the grace of this man of the Way; having heard the Dharma, I have been reborn in the heavens. I have now come to offer flowers as a token of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness!"
Therefore, when a person is at the point of death, those attending to them on their side must not fail to protect the patient’s mind.

(17) Once, there was a man in a foreign land who managed his livelihood; he brought forward several thousand *kiṅ* of gold and silver and held it in great esteem, wishing to bury it in the ground for fear that moles, insects, or rats might invade and steal it.
He wished to hide it in a marshy thicket, yet again feared that foxes or wild beasts might take it.
Furthermore, he did not believe in his family, relatives, wife, or children; he carried them in his heart as he went in and out, constantly fearing he might lose them.

During the month of the long fast, when disciples of the fourfold assembly all visited stupas and monasteries to burn incense and scatter flowers, this man observed and saw everything clearly in this manner.
Again, he saw before the stupa and temple a large alms bowl, around which the fourfold assembly of disciples was circumambulating, casting gold, silver, coins,
and valuables into the bowl. The man asked,
"Why are you casting these treasures into this bowl?"
The practitioner replied:
"This is called 'generosity,' the second is called 'secure storage,' and the third is called 'not knowing decay.
The man reflected:
"This is truly what such a person as you has said; it accords with what I seek.
He then took his gold and silver and cast it all into the bowl.
The practitioner offered a prayer of blessing and further said:

"That which is firm cannot be submerged by water, nor burned by fire; thieves and enemies cannot harm it, and even if cast into a treasure vault, it does not decay. In the future, one will obtain a reward hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater; therefore, it is called 'giving' (dāna)."
The man’s mind was awakened and he rejoiced immeasurably; he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna before the stupa.
Thus, when one performs meritorious deeds with a sincere heart, the effort is never in vain, and one will personally attain the Way.

18 (18). Formerly, at Kukkutārāma Monastery, there was an elder bhikṣu who had attained the path of arhatship. He was accompanied by a śrāmaṇera; from time to time they would descend to enter the city for sightseeing, and because his robes and bowl were very heavy, he had the śrāmaṇera carry them while following behind him.
While on the road, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"All people born into this world do not fail to experience suffering; if one wishes to escape this suffering, what kind of path should one cultivate?"
He thought to himself:
"The Buddha has always praised:
'The Bodhisattva is supreme!'"
"I shall now resolve to attain the Bodhisattva mind.
As soon as he had this thought, his teacher, using his knowledge of others' minds, clearly perceived what he was thinking and said to the śrāmaṇera:
"Bring your robes and bowl here."
The śrāmaṇera then took his robes and bowl and presented them to his preceptor.
The preceptor said to the śrāmaṇera, "You go ahead."
Just as the śrāmaṇera was walking ahead, he again thought to himself:

"The path of a bodhisattva involves immense toil and suffering; to give one's head when asked for a head, or one's eyes when asked for eyes—such matters are extremely difficult and beyond my capability. It would be better for me to attain arhatship early and quickly escape from suffering."
The Master, again perceiving what the śrāmaṇera was thinking, said to him:
"You, you, take your robes and bowl and follow behind me.
This he did three times, and the śrāmaṇera was struck with wonder and astonishment, not knowing the Master's intention.
When he arrived at his lodging, he joined his palms and addressed his teacher, inquiring about its meaning. The teacher replied:
"Because you advanced three times toward the Bodhisattva path, I likewise pushed you forward three times; because your mind retreated three times, I pushed you back."
The reason for this is that the merit of generating the bodhicitta surpasses that of filling the three thousandfold world-system with arhats; it is beyond all comparison.
19 (19) Once, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who both left the household life to become śramaṇas.
The elder brother delighted in observing the precepts and practicing dhyāna; he sought the Way with single-minded devotion but did not favor giving.
The younger brother delighted in practicing giving to cultivate merit, yet he took pleasure in violating the precepts.

When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, his elder brother encountered the Buddha, left the household life to practice the Way, and immediately attained arhatship; yet, being uniquely deficient in merit, he constantly suffered from a lack of food and clothing. While wandering with his companions to beg for alms, he alone would always return without having eaten his fill.

His younger brother was born as an elephant; possessing great strength, he was able to repel enemies and was beloved by the king. The king adorned his body with fine gold, silver, precious jewels, and necklaces, and granted him several hundred villages to provide for this elephant according to its every need.

The elder bhikṣu encountered a time of great famine in the world; he wandered for seven days begging for food without obtaining anything, until finally he received a small amount of coarse food that barely sustained his life. Knowing beforehand that this elephant was his brother from a previous life, he went before the elephant, grasped its ear with his hand, and said to it:
"Do you and I both have faults!"

The elephant then reflected upon the bhikṣu’s words and immediately attained the recollection of his past lives; seeing the causal conditions of his previous existence, he became sorrowful and ceased eating and drinking.
Terrified, the elephant calf went to inform the king, saying, "The elephant no longer eats or drinks; I do not know what his intention is.
The king questioned the elephant calf.
"Has anyone previously committed an offense against the elephant?
The elephant cub replied to the king, "There was no other person;
I saw only a single śramaṇa come to the side of the elephant and depart after a short while."
The king immediately dispatched men in all directions to search for this śramaṇa.
Someone found him among the trees in the forest and, having captured the śramaṇa, brought him before the king.
The king asked the śramaṇa,
"What did you say when you reached my elephant?
The śramaṇa replied to the king:
"I have nothing more to say; I simply told the elephant:
'I and you both bear guilt!

" At that time, the śramaṇa related the details of their past-life karmic causes and conditions to the king. The king’s mind was immediately awakened, and he immediately released the śramaṇa, allowing him to return to his dwelling.
Therefore, families who cultivate merit should practice both precepts and giving; one must not be biased or partial, lest their meritorious deeds remain incomplete.
(20) Once, there was a bhikṣu who had been expelled from the community; he walked along, lamenting in grief and weeping bitterly.
On the road he encountered a ghost; this ghost had violated the law and was likewise banished by King Vaiśravaṇa.
At that time, the ghost asked the bhikṣu:
"For what reason do you walk along weeping?"
The bhikṣu replied:

“I have committed an offense against the Saṃgha and have been expelled by the assembly of monks; I have lost all offerings from donors, and my ill repute has spread far and wide. For these reasons, I am grieving, lamenting, and weeping!”
The ghost said to the bhikṣu:

"I can cause you to extinguish your ill repute and enable you to receive great offerings. You should simply mount upon my left shoulder; I shall carry you away, suspended in mid-air. People will see only you and not my body. If you receive great offerings, you must first give some to me."
The ghost immediately carried the bhikṣu through the air above the village where he had previously been expelled.
When the villagers saw this, they were all struck with wonder and marvel, believing that he had attained the Way. They said to one another, "The Saṃgha has acted improperly;
they have unjustly expelled one who has attained the Way."

At that time, the people of the village all went to this monastery to rebuke the community of monks; they then brought this bhikṣu back and stationed him within the monastery, whereupon he received great offerings.
This bhikṣu, in accordance with his original vow, would always first give whatever food, clothing, or other requisites he obtained to the ghost.

On another day, as the ghost was again carrying this bhikṣu through the air, they happened upon the officials and subordinates of King Vaiśravaṇa. Upon seeing the king's attendants, the ghost became terrified; he hurled the bhikṣu away and fled with all his might. Consequently, the bhikṣu fell to the ground and died, his body and head shattered and mangled.

This metaphor illustrates that a practitioner should cultivate their own path with unwavering resolve; for those who rely on the power of the mighty may suddenly fall into ruin, no different from the former case.
(21) Once, Maudgalyāyana was descending from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain with his disciples to the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms.
While on the road, Maudgalyāyana looked up into the sky and sighed with regret.
His disciple asked, "For what reason do you sigh?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“If you wish to know, you must return to the Buddha’s presence and ask him.
Thereupon, having finished his almsround, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, and his disciple asked about the matter he had previously praised.

Maudgalyāyana replied: “I saw in the upper reaches of the void a hungry ghost whose body was extremely large and whose form was hideous. Seven glowing iron balls entered its mouth and passed straight through; once they had passed through, they re-entered the mouth. Its entire body was ablaze, and it writhed in agony. It fell prostrate and then rose up again, rising only to fall back down once more. It was for this reason that I sighed!”
"It is not that I alone have seen this; the Buddha has also seen it!
The disciple asked, "By what causes and conditions do you suffer in such a way?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"You yourself should ask this of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
His disciple immediately addressed the Buddha, inquiring about the causes and conditions.
Then the Buddha replied:

"This hungry ghost was once a śrāmaṇera in a previous life. At a time of extreme famine when people subsisted on beans, this śrāmaṇera was distributing food to the assembly of monks; when he reached his own teacher, he gave him seven extra beans. Because of this transgression, he has received such bitter suffering in the body of a hungry ghost."
The Buddha said, "I too have often seen why I do not speak [of this]: I fear that people would not believe it and would incur extremely heavy retribution!
This is like the analogy of those who possess few beans; because they act as teachers for others while not practicing themselves, their transgression is likewise grave!"

How much more so when one fails to give rise to faith upon hearing the Buddha preach the Prajñāpāramitā, but instead slanders it; such a person's transgression is heavier than the five heinous crimes, and they shall undergo the most extreme sufferings of hell for an incalculable length of time.

22 (22). Once there was a householder whose wife was pregnant. After he had invited the Buddha to his home and completed the offerings, he wished to have the Tathāgata divine whether the child his wife would later bear would be a boy or a girl.
The Buddha said:

"In the future, she shall give birth to a son who will be upright and handsome. Upon reaching adulthood, he shall experience celestial pleasures among human beings, and later he shall attain the path of Arhatship."
When the householder heard this, he was suspicious and did not believe it. Later, after he had again invited the six teachers and completed their offerings, he had them perform a divination as well.
The householder said to the six teachers:
"Previously, when I had the Śramaṇa Gautama perform a divination, he said:"
"He shall later give birth to a son.
Is he truly a boy?
The six masters replied:
"She shall give birth to a daughter.
Those six teachers and their followers, harboring hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha's Dharma and desiring to oppose it, reflected within themselves:
"If she gives birth to a son, this householder will surely abandon us and serve Gautama."
He then spoke deceptively to the householder, saying:

"Your wife shall give birth to a son; however, after the son is born, there will be great misfortune, and your family and relatives will perish for seven generations. Because it would have been inauspicious, I previously spoke falsely, saying it was a daughter."
Upon hearing this, the householder was greatly terrified and did not know what to do.
The six heretical teachers then said to the householder:
"If you wish for good fortune and prosperity, you must simply remove it."

The six teachers then pressed the belly of the householder’s wife, intending to cause her to miscarry; instead, they harmed her mother, so that the householder’s wife subsequently died while the child did not.
"It is due to the merit of his past lives!

The householder then abandoned his wife at the place where the corpse lay, piled up a great quantity of firewood, and set it ablaze. As the flames grew intense, the Buddha, accompanied by his disciples, went to observe the scene.

As soon as the householder’s wife was destroyed, she saw her son sitting upon a lotus flower, upright and beautiful, with a countenance as pure as snow; the Buddha then commanded Jīvaka to bring this child here.

Jīvaka entered the fire, carried the child out, and returned him to his original lay patron; he was subsequently raised until, at the age of sixteen, his talent and beauty surpassed those of others. Thereupon, he prepared a great variety of exquisite foods and drinks and invited the six teachers.
Not long after the six teachers had taken their seats, they suddenly burst into laughter.
One of them asked, "For what reason do you laugh?
The six teachers replied:
"I saw a mountain fifty thousand *li* away with water at its base; a monkey fell into the water, and that is why I laughed!
Knowing this was a falsehood, the boy took various kinds of fine soup in his bowl, covered it with rice, and had someone carry it to the man.
In the bowls of the others, rice was placed at the bottom and soup on top; everyone ate, but the Six Teachers alone were angry and would not eat.
The host asked, "Why do you not eat?"
The six teachers replied, "There is no soup; how can we eat?
The host said:
"You can see a monkey fifty thousand *li* away falling into the water with your eyes; why do you not see the soup falling onto the rice?
Thereupon, the six masters became greatly enraged and returned without eating at all.
The layman and his son, because of this, ceased their service [to the false teacher] and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

The Buddha preached the Dharma to them in various ways, whereupon they attained the fruits of the Path. This parable is extremely numerous; I have recorded it briefly to clarify how the true and the false are distinguished in this manner.
