(23) [Sutra 23] In a foreign land, there was a master of dragon-subduing spells who, carrying a water jar filled with water, went to the edge of a dragon pond and recited the incantations with single-minded concentration. Immediately, this dragon saw a great fire arise from the bottom of the pond, so that the entire body of water blazed up.

The dragon, terrified by the fire, raised its head to look toward the mountain; it then saw a great conflagration burning all the mountains and marshes. Looking up at the mountain peak, he saw it was empty with no place to dwell. As everything was ablaze and there was no ground for him to rest upon, he saw only the water in the bathing jar where he might find refuge. He then extinguished his massive body, assumed a minute form, and entered the water within the jar.

That dragon pond is a metaphor for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); the mountain and marshes one gazes upon are metaphors for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); looking at the mountain peak is a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the master who subdues the dragon is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva; the water in the ritual jar is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*; the incantation is a metaphor for skillful means (*upāya*); the great fire that blazes is a metaphor for manifesting impermanence; the dragon’s large body is a metaphor for arrogance; and its transformation into a small form is a metaphor for humility.

It is said that the Bodhisattva manifests the conflagration of the kalpa, showing that the realms of desire and form are likewise consumed; by terrifying sentient beings with the great fire of impermanence, he causes them to eliminate arrogance and become humble and lowly, after which they all enter nirvana.

24 (Twenty-fourth): Once, a fowler spread a net across a marsh and placed food that birds eat within it. A flock of birds, calling to their companions, vied with one another to come and eat it; the fowler then pulled the net, and all the birds fell into the mesh.
At that time, there was a large and powerful bird that lifted this net with its body and flew away together with the flock. The fowler, seeing their shadow, pursued them on foot.
Someone said to the fowler, "The birds fly through the void while you pursue them on foot; how foolish you are!"
The bird-teacher replied:
"It was not as you told me; those birds, seeking to roost at dusk, were intent on different goals, and thus they shall fall."

The man continued to pursue them without ceasing, and as the sun was already setting, he looked up at the flock of birds flying about, competing and struggling; some were heading east, others west, some toward the long forest, and others toward the mountain ravines. Their competitive struggle did not cease for even a moment before they fell, and the bird-trapper caught them one by one in order and killed them.
The bird-catcher is like Pāpīyān;
the spreading of the net is like the fetters (*saṃyojana*);
and carrying the net while flying is like a person who has not yet abandoned the fetters and seeks to find the essential way out.
Ceasing at sunset is like a person who becomes indolent and no longer advances;
seeking different places to roost is like giving rise to the sixty-two views that contradict one another;
and the birds falling to the ground is like a person receiving false retribution by falling into hell.
This clarifies that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and defilements (*rajas*) constitute the net of Māra; thus, the fetters enshroud a person just like a web.
Between these two paths, one should diligently guard body and speech with what is wholesome, lest one become heedless and remain within this net.
The suffering of the three evil realms and the long duration of birth and death are unbearable states.

(25) [Sutra 25] Once there were five hundred merchants who, embarking upon a ship, entered the sea seeking precious treasures. They encountered the great Makara fish, which raised its head and opened its mouth, intending to devour all living beings.
At that time, the wind was sharp and the ship sped like an arrow;
the merchant leader said to the crowd, "The ship is moving too fast; we should lower the sails and let it drift.
They immediately did as he said, lowering the sails and letting it drift, yet the ship continued to move so swiftly that it could not be stopped.
The merchant leader asked the men on board,
"What do you see? They replied:
"I see two suns rising above me; beneath the suns are white mountains, and between them are black mountains.
The merchant leader said in alarm, "This must be a great fish; what shall we do?"

"We and you have now encountered this dire calamity; having entered the belly of this fish, there is no possibility of survival. Each of you should, according to whom you serve, single-mindedly seek deliverance.
Thereupon, the multitude each followed their respective objects of devotion, taking refuge with one-pointed mind to seek escape from this peril.
The more earnest their prayers became, the faster the boat sped away; before long, it was unstoppable and was about to enter the mouth of the fish.
Thereupon, the merchant leader addressed the people, saying:
"I have a great deity named Buddha; each of you, set aside what you are holding and with single-minded devotion, invoke his name!"
At that time, the five hundred people all raised their voices together, crying out:
"Namo Buddha! Hearing the name of the Buddha, the fish reflected within itself, saying:
"Today there is once again a Buddha in the world; how could I bear to harm sentient beings further?

As soon as he had this thought, he immediately closed his mouth, and the water flowed backward and receded far from the fish's mouth, so that the five hundred merchants were all at once delivered from their peril.

This fish had previously been a practitioner of the Way; because of a minor transgression, he received this fish form. Upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, he immediately recollected his past lives, and thus, through reflection, a virtuous mind was instantly born within him.

This clarifies that these five hundred merchants, by simply focusing their minds on the Buddha and briefly reciting his name, immediately attained liberation from a calamity as vast as the heavens; how much more so for those who uphold the *nien-fo samādhi*, which causes heavy offenses to become light and light ones to be extinguished—this is sufficient proof.
26 (26). Once there was a butcher who went to King Ajātaśatru and begged for one wish.
The king asked, "What wish do you seek?"
He replied, “At the time of festivals, it is necessary to slaughter animals; if Your Majesty grants me this favor, I shall perform them all.
The king said:
"Killing is something that people do not delight in; why do you seek it with such pleasure?

He replied, "In the past, I was a poor man who supported myself by working at a sheep-slaughterer's stall. Because of this, I was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings. When my lifespan in that heaven ended, I was reborn among humans, where I continued slaughtering sheep. After my life there ended, I was reborn in the second heaven."

In this manner, he slaughtered sheep six times; because of these deeds, he was reborn throughout the six heavens, where he enjoyed immeasurable blessings. For this reason, he now begs a single boon from the King.
The king said, "If it were as you say, how would one know it?
He replied:
"I remember my past lives.
When the king heard this, he did not believe it and called it a falsehood, saying:
"How could such a lowly person as this know his past lives?"
Later, he questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha replied: "It is indeed as you have said; it is no falsehood!

In a previous life, this person encountered a Pratyekabuddha. Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy and observed him with a sincere mind, looking up at his head and down at his feet. A virtuous mind immediately arose within him. By virtue of this merit, he was reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm. He returned to the human world six times, recognizing his own past lives. Because his merit had matured, he obtained six successive births among humans and devas; because his transgressions had not yet matured, he has not yet had to undergo suffering."

Only after this body perishes shall he enter hell to undergo the retribution for slaughtering sheep; once his hellish punishment is exhausted, he shall be reborn among sheep to repay his debt one by one.

Because this person’s knowledge of past lives is shallow, seeing only the affairs of the six heavens and failing to reach back to his seventh previous life, he concludes that slaughtering sheep is itself the cause for birth in heaven.
"Thus, merely knowing one's past lives is neither a supernormal power (*abhijñā*) nor an enlightenment (*vidyā*).
Therefore, those who cultivate merit must certainly make vows; do not act recklessly so that the karmic fruition remains obscure—this may serve as proof!
27 (27) Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“The Buddha was born into a royal family; having sat beneath a tree for six years contemplating the Way, he attained Buddhahood. Is it so easy to attain such a state?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, there was an elder who lived in great wealth with every kind of treasure fully provided; yet, lacking red pearls, he felt it was insufficient, and so he sent men into the sea to gather them."

Having endured hardships and perils, he finally reached the place where the treasure lay; he pierced his own body to draw out blood, which he wrapped in an oil-skin bag and suspended at the bottom of the sea. When the pearl-oysters smelled the fragrance of the blood, they came to feed upon it, and thus he was able to extract the oysters.
He split oyster shells to extract pearls, and after three years of gathering them, he finally obtained one to wear as a pendant.

When he returned to the seashore, his companions saw that he had acquired such a fine treasure and plotted together to seize it. They all went to fetch water, pushed him into a well, covered him over, and departed.

Having fallen to the bottom of the well for a long time, the man saw a lion coming from a side hole to drink water; the man was again filled with terror, but after the lion had departed, he found the opening and emerged, returning to his own land.
When her companion returned home, she called out to him, saying:
"You obtained one of my pendants; no one knows of it, and you even intended to harm me. You may secretly return it to me entirely, and I shall never speak of you!"
The man, terrified and trembling, returned all the pearls.
Having received them, the owner took them back home; his two sons wore the pearls and played together, asking one another:
"Where did these pearls originate?"
One child said,
"I was born from within a sack.
Another child said:
"He was born inside a jar.
When the father saw this, he laughed at him, whereupon the wife asked,
"Why do you laugh?"
He replied, "I obtained this pearl through such great toil and hardship; yet this child, having received it from me, does not recognize its origin and claims it was born inside a jar."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You see only me having attained Buddhahood, but you do not know the diligent suffering of my training throughout countless kalpas; that I have now attained it is what I call 'easy,' just as that infant thinks the pearl was born within his own pouch!"
Therefore, the cultivation of all myriad practices and the accumulation of merit over kalpas cannot be achieved through a single matter, a single action, or a single lifetime alone!
(28) Once, there was a guide who entered the sea to gather treasures; at that time, five hundred people followed him on the journey. The guide said to them:
"Within the sea there are five perils: [text continues]"
First is the turbulent current, second is the eddy, third is the great fish, fourth is the female demon, and fifth is the intoxicating fruit.
Only those capable of crossing these perils may travel together with me.
When the group had finished their preparations, they set sail with the wind and reached the Isle of Jewels, where each went to gather treasures.
One man, unable to resist the fragrance of the fruits, ate them and became intoxicated for seven days.
When the multitude of Jewel-Foot had arrived by means of the wind-sail, they prepared to return; they beat drums to assemble the people, yet not even one person was found among the four quarters.
Seeing him lying beneath a tree, intoxicated and still unawakened, they together carried him back, propping him up with split tree branches, and returned home to their kingdom.
The entire family, hearing of the auspicious news, all came out to welcome him; however, the one who had been intoxicated, seeing that he had gained nothing, was particularly distressed.
The drunken man, feeling unhappy, leaned on his staff as he entered the market. A merchant offered two ten-thousand taels of gold for it, which the man accepted. The merchant asked:
"What virtue does this staff possess?"
He replied, "This is a Tree-Jewel; if one pounds and burns this staff, it can fumigate all tiles and stones so that they are entirely transformed into precious jewels.

The man went back to seek it, and taking a small amount with him to test it, he found that it was indeed as he had been told: everything that was fumigated was completely transformed into various kinds of jewels.
The analogy states:
"The guide refers to the Bodhisattva;
the five difficulties refer to the five aggregates (pañca-skandha)."
The "jewel island" refers to the seven treasures of *prajñā*;
"the intoxicated" refers to those whose minds have become lax and negligent;
"breaking off branches from the jewel trees" refers to one's own diligent cultivation.
"To further arouse diligence so that tiles and stones are perfumed and become jewels means to perfume all evil deeds with the Way of the Sūtras so that they all become vessels of the Dharma!
(29) Formerly, in a mountain, there were two śramaṇas who dwelt in seclusion practicing the Path and attained the six supernormal powers.
Not far from there, a lioness had given birth to two cubs.
As they grew gradually larger, the mother lioness wished to go out; she reflected that only the two monks possessed the Way and virtue and could be entrusted with her life.
She then said, "I wish to go out, but my two cubs are still small and I fear someone might harm them; I wish to entrust them to you, O practitioners of the Way."
"If you would only grant me your compassionate protection, I shall naturally come to visit you.
The practitioner granted his request.
When Siṃha returned, he saw that his son had attached himself to the practitioner and had again abandoned him to go on his way.
When the practitioner returned from his almsround, they shared what remained of his food. Every time they saw him returning, they joyfully went out to welcome him.

Later, as the practitioner was walking along, he encountered a hunter; the lion cub bolted into the grass. Relying upon the practitioner, the hunter put on the *kāṣāya* robe from within the hut and entered the grass to capture it.

The lion, thinking him to be a man of the Way, immediately came out to meet him; the hunter struck and killed it, flayed its skin, and made a cloak from the lion's hide, which was worth a thousand taels of gold.

When the practitioner returned, he did not see the lion; sitting in meditation to contemplate it, he knew it had been killed by a hunter. He immediately used his supernormal powers to seize the skin and bring it back, making a cushion upon which he sat. Reciting incantations and prayers, he again sat in meditative contemplation and knew that he would be reborn in a wealthy family as twin sons.
The practitioner went to his house and asked the elder,
"What is it that you lack?
He replied:
"I only worry that I have no son.
He then reported this as his request for a son from the elder.
The elder was greatly delighted, and the practitioner said:
"If you obtain a son, how will you repay me?
He replied,
"When the son grows up, I shall offer him as a novice monk."
The practitioner said,
"Do not forget this essential point.
She merely felt that she was pregnant, and later indeed gave birth to twin sons who were identical to one another.
When the children were eight or nine years old, a practitioner of the Way passed by. Upon seeing him, the two boys felt spontaneous joy. The practitioner said to the elder:
"Do you recognize your original vow?"
The elder did not dare to violate his vow and immediately bestowed his two sons upon the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa took them into the mountains to study, and before long, they also attained arhatship.

Furthermore, because he constantly sat upon his own skin, he would enter into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) every day to observe himself. Thereupon, he saw the skins from his previous lives, each of which rose up to pay him homage and express gratitude:
"It is by the power of the Master's grace that we have attained the Way; this is entirely due to the power of your compassionate mindfulness."
"If even birds and beasts with virtuous hearts can attain liberation, how much more so for those whose aspirations and emotions are directed toward making wholesome vows?
(30) Once there was a butcher who wished to make offerings to a practitioner of the Way, but because of his evil nature, no one would go to him."

Later, he saw a newly ordained śramaṇa whose deportment was dignified and orderly; he invited him to his home for a meal of various delicacies. When the meal was finished, he again invited the practitioner, saying:
"I pray that you will accept meals at my house for the rest of your life."
The practitioner immediately accepted it.
Having practiced it for a long time, he repeatedly saw the butcher killing living beings right before him, yet he did not dare to rebuke him.
After many years had passed, the butcher’s father died and became a ghost in the river; he would cut his own body with a knife and then immediately restore it to its former state.
As a practitioner of the Way was crossing a river, a ghost seized the boat and said,
"Only by sinking this practitioner into the river can you depart.
The boatman, struck with fear, said:

The ghost said, "In the past, my family made offerings to this practitioner; for many years he did not rebuke me for killing living beings. Now that I am suffering this calamity, I desire [to kill him] out of resentment!"
The boatman said,
"If even those who kill living beings suffer such calamity, how much more so for a practitioner of the Way?
The ghost said:
"I know it is only because of your anger!
If you can perform an act of merit for me by giving alms and reciting prayers in my name, I shall release you.
The boatmen all agreed to perform the meritorious rite, and the ghost then released them.

The practitioner immediately held a memorial service for the ghosts, calling out their names and reciting prayers of blessing; the others followed in succession by holding services and going to the river to call out to the ghosts, saying:
"Have you received any blessings yet?"
The ghost said, "It has been obtained; there shall be no further pain.
The boatman said:
"I shall perform meritorious deeds for you tomorrow; will you be able to come in person?
The ghost replied, "I shall."

At dawn, the ghost transformed himself into the likeness of a Brahmin and came; he personally made offerings with his own hands and received the blessing of the incantation. The Elder preached the sutra for him, and the ghost immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna. He departed in great joy.

Therefore, when it is appropriate for the host or guest to offer correction through reasoned admonition, even if one has fallen into evil paths, there remains the possibility of wholesome conditions; thus it can be said that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition!
31. Once there was a merchant who entered the sea to gather treasures. He encountered a great nāga deity who raised up the ship, intending to capsize it, and all the people were struck with terror.
The nāga said,
"Do you ever travel to that country?
They replied:
"I have traveled there before," [the dragon said].
He gave [the king] a large egg, the size of a five-sheng jar, saying:
"Take this egg and bury it beneath a great tree in the marketplace of that kingdom; if you do not, I shall kill you later."
The man consented.
Later, he passed through that country and buried the eggs beneath a large tree in the marketplace.
From that time forward, the kingdom suffered many calamities, diseases, and pestilence.
The king summoned a master of esoteric arts to perform a divination, who declared that there was a python’s egg within the kingdom, which was causing the pestilence.
He immediately ordered it to be excavated and burned; consequently, all the illnesses were completely cured.
The merchant followed behind his companions into the sea, whereupon he encountered the dragon deity, who questioned him again regarding the circumstances of the matter. The merchant replied:

"Formerly, as the deity instructed, we buried the eggs in the marketplace; consequently, there was much pestilence in the kingdom. The King summoned a Brahmin to perform divination, and he deduced that by burning them, the disease would be entirely eliminated."
The deity said,
"I regret that I did not kill those slaves.
The boatmen asked the deity:
"Why is it so? The deity said,
"Have you ever heard of a certain strong man named So-and-So from a certain country?"
He replied,
"I have heard that he has already passed away!
The spirit said:

"It is I! While I was alive, I delighted in oppressing the people of the kingdom; no one ever instructed or rebuked me, but only encouraged me, causing me to fall among the pythons with the intent to slaughter them all!"

Therefore, people should admonish one another to follow what is good and accord with one another; do not rely on your own power and influence to oppress others, for by doing so you will sit and invite calamity—the suffering of the three evil realms. You may hear their voices, but you must not dwell in their physical forms.
32 (Thirty-two). Formerly, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there were five hundred blind men who wandered about begging for alms. Encountering a time of famine, they obtained nothing;
they deliberated among themselves, saying, "The Buddha resides in Śrāvastī teaching people the practice of giving. We should go to that kingdom so that we may save our lives."
Each said, "We should hire one person to lead us to that place.
The five hundred blind men each promised one silver coin, and the man agreed to take them to that country; they then set out on their journey.
The hired man said to the blind men, "This path below is perilous;
each of you give me some money, and if we encounter bandits, I shall hide it for you."
The blind men gave all their money to him, and having received it, the man departed immediately.
After wandering for several days, the blind men became hungry and thirsty and could no longer find the way; they then simultaneously took refuge in the Buddha, saying:
"O Holy and Divine Buddha, please have compassion on us and deliver us from this calamity."
The Buddha then suddenly manifested his divine power before them; he stroked the heads of the blind with his hand, and they all regained their sight, their hunger and thirst being fully satisfied.
The five hundred people rejoiced and leaped for joy, vowing to become his disciples; their hair and beards fell away instantly, and they were clothed in robes, bowls, and the dharma-garments.
The Buddha again preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained arhatship; they then flew along with the Buddha back to the Jetavana Monastery.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What sins or merits did these five hundred people possess in their past lives?"

The Buddha said, "In a past life, there was an elder who hired five hundred men for labor. He first took their wages and scattered them away, and only afterward did he make them work. Because of this transgression across successive lifetimes, they have now suffered this calamity."
"The elder who was carrying away the money at that time is this very person!
Having been released from his debt, he encountered my awakening; now he has attained the Way.
Such are the workings of sin and merit; therefore, as the karmic actions people create differ—whether they be the karma of creation or the karma of retribution—one must not fail to be careful."
33 (Thirty-three): In the past, there were two men who were close relatives and friends, never at odds with one another.
Later, one of them committed a crime for which the penalty was death; he then fled and passed by his friend.
Jñānaprasthāna did not open the door and asked in return,
"Who are you? He replied:
"I am indeed a scholar; it is only because I have committed a crime that I have come to visit you.
The man replied, "One acts as a kinsman in times of leisure, but when faced with an emergency, each must go their own way; I will not precede you!"
His close friend was deeply distressed and thought to himself:
"When people are at ease, they come and go together, eating and drinking without ever parting; why then, in times of urgency, do you abandon me like this?"
"Is this not being too kind?
he thought, and was about to depart for the mountains.
Then another spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) passed by; the man opened the door and hid him, saying:
"Although you are but a stranger to me, I shall see that you are established in a place of safety.

He then loaded precious treasures onto a carriage and traveled himself to another country, where he informed the king and the local elders of his arrival. For him, he constructed a palace and provided him with fields, houses, and wealth; having supplied these, he took his leave and returned home.
At that time, the Buddha, seeing this person, drew an analogy:
"The offender represents the spirit; the kinsmen and friends represent the body composed of the four great elements."
A virtuous friend is analogous to the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

It is like a person who nourishes the four great elements with food, drink, and the four requisites without lack; yet when Impermanence arrives, they must fall into the evil realms. Seeking a place to hide, they find that for even a moment the gates are closed and they cannot advance.

Later, he encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who takes him to another country and provides all that is necessary so that he lacks for nothing. This is a metaphor for how the power of merit—derived from practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts—draws one to the heavens at the time of death; there, one dwells in palaces of the seven treasures, wears celestial jeweled robes, and enjoys heavenly food of a hundred flavors, reaching the ultimate state of immeasurable bliss.

Therefore, when one is born into this world, one should not consume food merely for self-sustenance; rather, one should practice austerity and cultivate merit. For what benefit is there in merely nourishing the four great elements of the body? Those who understand this should put it into practice!

34 (34). One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, there was a king who served the celestial deities. He performed a great sacrificial rite, offering one hundred heads each of oxen, sheep, pigs, boars, dogs, and chickens. He entrusted all of them to the kitchen attendants to slaughter the oxen and sheep.
Among the kitchen attendants was an upāsaka who said,
"I uphold the Buddha's precepts and may not take life.
The head cook became greatly enraged and immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to punish him.
The King asked,
"Do you truly intend to disobey my command?"
"I shall kill you!
The cook replied, "I am a disciple of the Buddha who upholds the five precepts; I would rather take my own life than violate the Buddha's teachings by killing a living being."

If one commits murder in accordance with the King’s command, they shall die and enter hell; after billions of years, when their retribution is exhausted, they will emerge, yet they shall always be short-lived.

If one maintains the precepts without flaw and is executed by the King, upon death they shall ascend to the heavens; there they shall obtain blessings and their wishes shall be spontaneously fulfilled. Even if one must now face death, this present body shall be transformed into a celestial existence. The distance between the retributions of sin and merit is thus exceedingly vast.
"For this reason, I shall die rather than violate [my word]!
The king said, "I grant you a period of seven days; I shall have an elephant trample you to death. If you do not die, your words shall indeed be true."

After seven days, all the men had become upāsakas; they manifested the physical marks of a Buddha and assumed the form of a Buddha to verify that five hundred elephants had previously trodden upon them.

The upāsaka, in accordance with the Buddha’s Dharma, raised his five fingers which were transformed into the Five Sacred Mountains; from between each mountain a lion emerged. Upon seeing the lions, the elephants were struck with terror and all prostrated themselves upon the ground, just as they did when the Buddha was alive.
The king then came to believe that there was indeed a Buddha and immediately ceased his sacrificial rites.
From that time on, he received the Buddha's precepts; his ministers, officials, and the people likewise all received the precepts from him, and he subsequently became the national teacher.
The wise maintain the precepts and deliver others in this manner.
(35) Once, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a laywoman who visited the Buddha morning and evening to make offerings with such utmost devotion that she never grew weary.
The Buddha, knowing [his thoughts], asked:
"What is your aspiration?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a reward for my merit, I wish to give birth to four sons in this present life.
The Buddha then asked,
"Why do you seek four sons?"
The upāsikā said:

"When my four sons have grown up, I shall have one manage the livelihood through trade and commerce to accumulate wealth and treasures; I shall have another oversee agriculture and animal husbandry to accumulate livestock and grain; I shall have another seek office to receive a salary and provide protection for our household; and I wish to have one leave the home life to become a śramaṇa, attain the Way, and upon its accomplishment, return to deliver his parents and all people—it is precisely for this purpose that I seek these four sons!"
The Buddha said,
"I shall cause you to obtain your wish.
The upāsikā was greatly rejoiced, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Later, she gave birth to a son who was intelligent and wise; his mother loved him beyond compare in this world.
When the son had grown up, he asked his mother:
"Why is your loving affection so excessive? There has never been its equal."
The mother said to her son, "I originally vowed for four sons;
I have obtained only you, one person. My love is concentrated entirely upon you, and that is why it is so.
She then explained her underlying intentions to her son in full detail.
Upon hearing his mother’s words, the son was deeply moved by her resolve; he immediately went forth to engage in business and, before a year had passed, acquired hundreds of millions in wealth.
Next, he established agricultural estates and livestock, possessing countless oxen, horses, cattle, and grain.
Subsequently, he pursued learning and entered official service to seek office; he took a wife, fathered sons, and his household eventually became a prosperous and influential family.
He spoke again, saying:

"The reason I sought these four sons was because each knew one particular skill; now that they act on my behalf, three tasks are roughly accomplished, and only one remains lacking. It would be most excellent if one of them could leave the household life."
The compassionate mother said,
"The wishes of my four sons have been fulfilled!
Then the mother thought to herself:

"Each of the four sons entrusted by my original vow was given a single task, yet I feared they might not accomplish it; what this child has achieved exceeds my expectations, and if he is permitted to leave the household life, he will surely attain the Way."
He immediately granted permission for his son to leave the household life.

The son took leave of his mother and went to the Buddha’s dwelling to request ordination as a śramaṇa; he immediately attained full diligence and, before long, realized the path of an arhat. He returned to deliver his parents and all other people, so that everyone who obtained merit and the Way was filled with joy.
Therefore, when one creates merit and makes vows, it depends solely upon the mind and intention; there is nothing that cannot be attained.

(36) Once there was an old woman who had only one son. When he fell ill and passed away, she carried his corpse to the cemetery and laid it down, overcome with such grief that she could not control herself:
"I had this one son to provide for my old age, yet he has abandoned me to die. What use is my life now?"
"We can no longer return; we shall meet our end together in this one place.
Having neither eaten nor drunk for four or five days, the Buddha, knowing their state, went with five hundred bhikṣus to that cemetery.

The old woman saw the Buddha approaching from afar; his majestic spiritual power radiated brilliantly, causing those who were deluded to awaken and those who were intoxicated to sober up. She went forward to pay homage to the Buddha and stood before him.
The Buddha asked the old woman, "Why are you here among the graves?"
She addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have but one son who has passed away after leaving me; my love for him is so profound that I wish to die in the same place as he.
The Buddha told the old woman:
"Do you wish for your son to live again?
The mother said,
"Excellent!"
He replied,
"I wish to obtain it!
The Buddha said:
"I shall seek incense and fire so that I may offer prayers for rebirth.
He said to his elderly mother,
"In seeking fire, you should obtain the 'fire of the household' which brings immortality."
Thereupon, the old woman went to fetch fire; whenever she saw someone, she would ask:
"Has there been anyone who has died in your household, either before or after?
They replied:
"Since time immemorial, our ancestors have all died.
This was the answer he received at every place he inquired.
After passing through dozens of households without daring to take fire, he returned to the Buddha’s presence and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: [The rest of his report follows.]
"Though one searches everywhere for fire, there is no one who does not die; therefore, you have returned empty-handed.
The Buddha told the old woman:
"Since the beginning of heaven and earth, there has been no birth that does not end."
"When a person dies, what joy is there for those who remain behind?
Why, Mother, are you so deluded as to seek to follow your son in death?
At these words, the mother’s mind was relieved, and she came to understand the principle of impermanence.

The Buddha, for this reason, extensively expounded the Dharma for him; he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Among the several thousand people who were observing from the cemetery, many conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.
37 (Thirty-seven). Once there was a man who had two wives.
The elder wife had no children, while the younger wife gave birth to a son who was handsome and lovely; her husband rejoiced greatly.

The senior wife harbored jealousy within her heart, yet outwardly she feigned a love for him that surpassed even that for her own son. When the boy was about one year old, everyone in the household knew that the senior wife cherished him deeply, and no longer entertained any doubts.

The eldest wife pricked the child’s palate with a needle until it pierced through the skin and flesh; the child fell ill and cried out, refusing to nurse, so that none of the family members, young or old, knew the cause. On the seventh day, he died.

The elder wife also wept, and the younger wife, consumed by grief, wailed day and night without ceasing; she no longer took food or drink and was on the verge of death. Later, she realized she had been wronged by the elder wife and desired to take revenge.
He went to a stupa and monastery and asked the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones, if one wishes to fulfill the aspirations of the heart, what merit should one cultivate?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Those who seek their heart's desires should observe the eight precepts of the *poṣadha*; then what they seek will be fulfilled as they wish.
Having received the eight precepts from the bhikṣu, he departed; seven days later, he died.
She was reborn as the eldest wife’s daughter, beautiful and well-proportioned; the eldest wife doted on her, but she died at the age of one year.
The eldest wife sat upright and refused to eat, her grief and lamentation being even more intense than that of the younger wife.

In this manner, after seven cycles—whether two years, three years, four or five years, or six or seven years—she subsequently became increasingly beautiful and far more excellent than before. When she was finally fourteen years old and betrothed to a man, just as she was about to leave her home, she suddenly passed away that very night.

The senior wife wept and lamented in such unbearable grief that she could no longer speak and ceased eating or drinking; day and night she walked about shedding tears as she wailed, refusing to close the coffin where the corpse lay, gazing upon the body every day, its radiant countenance appearing even more beautiful than when it was alive.
After more than twenty days, an arhat, seeing him and wishing to deliver him, went to his house to beg for alms.
He had a maidservant bring a bowl of rice and offer it to him, but he refused to accept it, saying to the maid:
"I wish to see your master."
The maidservant returned and reported,
"She wishes to see the mistress.
She replied:
"I am suffering from grief and on the verge of death; how could I go out to see the śramaṇa?
You should take these goods and give them to him so that he will depart.
The maidservant took the goods and gave them to the śramaṇa, yet he still refused to leave.
The śramaṇa said, "I wish to see the master.

Although the maidservant repeated this several times, the śramaṇa did not leave. The wife became distressed and despondent; as the śramaṇa remained standing there without departing, he disturbed her mind and she could no longer endure it, so she spoke:
"Call her here!
When the śramaṇa saw the woman before him, her complexion was haggard, she was covering her face with her hands, and she had not combed her hair for some time.
The śramaṇa asked, "Why have you come to such a state?"
The wife said, "In the past and present, seven daughters have been born to me; though they were clever and lovely, they died.
This daughter was the eldest, and as she was about to leave for marriage, she too died, causing me great sorrow."
The śramaṇa said, "I shall speak to you once I have combed my hair and wiped my face.
The woman continued to weep and refused to stop; the śramaṇa then said to her:
"Where is your young wife now?
For what reason did she originally die?
When the woman heard these words, she thought to herself:
"What cause does this śramaṇa have for knowing this?
His mind felt slightly better.
The śramaṇa spoke, saying:
“Gather your hair together, and I shall explain it to you!
Once the woman had finished binding her hair, the śramaṇa said:
“How did your young son die?”
Upon hearing these words, the wife remained silent and did not answer; she felt ashamed in her heart and did not dare speak further.
The śramaṇa said:

"You killed your son, causing his mother to die of grief, anxiety, and anguish. Therefore, I have come to be your son for seven successive lifetimes; I am your enemy, wishing to kill you with the poison of sorrow."
"Go and examine the dead girl in the coffin; see whether she is still intact or not?
The woman went to look at her, and found her already putrid and rotten, so foul-smelling that one could not approach her.
He asked:
"Why do you remember it?
The woman immediately felt ashamed and buried it; she then sought mercy from the śramaṇa, wishing to receive the precepts.
The śramaṇa said:
"Come to the monastery tomorrow.
After the woman died, she was reborn as a venomous snake; knowing that her former wife was about to go and receive the precepts, she waited for her along the road, intending to bite and kill her.
As the woman walked, the snake blocked her path so that she could not proceed; as the sun was about to set, the woman became greatly terrified and thought to herself:
"I wish to go to the śramaṇa’s place to receive the precepts; why does this snake block my way, preventing me from going?"
The śramaṇa knew this and went to where the woman was.
Upon seeing the śramaṇa, the woman was overjoyed and stepped forward to pay her respects. The śramaṇa said to the snake:

"In life after life, you have repeatedly become the junior wife of others, inflicting mutual cruelty and malice that can never be exhausted. You have caused a senior wife in the present world to kill her son once; now you have already suffered remorse seven times. Your past and present transgressions and evils may all be brought to an end."
"This woman is now going to receive the precepts; you have cut off her path. You shall enter the niraya hells for lifetime after lifetime without end.
Now that you appear in the body of a snake, how can it compare to this woman's body?"

Upon hearing the words of the śramaṇa, the snake came to know its own past lives; filled with resentment and distress, it prostrated its head upon the ground and remained motionless, contemplating the śramaṇa’s words.
The śramaṇa offered this benediction:

“Now that you two have mutually exhausted your afflictions from past lives, your transgressions shall hereafter be fully ended; henceforth, in every lifetime, do not again harbor ill will toward one another.”
When both had finished their repentance, the snake immediately passed away and was reborn among human beings.

At that time, having listened to the words of the śramaṇa, its mind opened and its understanding was clarified; filled with joy, it attained the stage of Srotāpanna. It then followed the śramaṇa to receive the precepts and became an upāsikā.
Therefore, since the retribution for sinful karma is such as this, one must not fail to exercise caution.
(38) Once, in the city of Śrāvastī, it rained blood for a distance of forty li in both length and breadth.

The king and his ministers were greatly astonished and marveled at this; they immediately summoned various practitioners of esoteric arts and those skilled in divination to determine whether it portended good or ill fortune.
The diviners replied:
"An ancient record states:..."
"The calamity of raining blood portends the birth of a man-eating python or a venomous creature.
It is fitting that you investigate within the kingdom to identify the source of this disaster.
The King said:
"How can this be distinguished? The diviner replied:
"This person is poisonous and difficult to distinguish; let us try by ordering all the newborn infants in the kingdom to be brought here, and have each spit into an empty jar."
Among them, one child spat into a jar, and it immediately burst into flames; they knew this child was a human-nāga.
They deliberated and said, "He must not be kept among humans," and so they moved him to a secluded, uninhabited place in the wilderness.
"Whoever in the kingdom is destined to die should be sent to him.
The python spat venom and killed them; in this manner, seventy-two thousand people were killed by his venom over time.
A lion arrived and let out a thunderous roar; within a distance of forty *li*, all people were struck with terror and submission, and its violent ravages could not be restrained.
Thereupon, the king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, offering one thousand pieces of gold and the fief of a county to anyone capable of repelling the lion.
There was no one who could respond.
The ministers said to the king:
"Only a person of extraordinary capacity would be able to repel him."
He immediately ordered his officials to go and summon the man-ogre.

From afar, they saw the lion go straight toward him and stand before him; the ogre blew forth a poisonous breath, and the lion died instantly. The ogre’s body rotted away, and the kingdom attained peace and tranquility.

Later, when the human python was old and fell ill, his life was about to end. The Buddha, pitying him for his heavy transgressions and the fact that he would surely fall into an evil realm from which there would be no time of escape, addressed Śāriputra:
"Go and exhort him so that he may be delivered from this grave calamity."
Śāriputra then went to her home; by means of his supernormal powers, he entered and suddenly stood before her.
The human-nāga Loṅnu thought to herself:
"I have not yet passed away, yet I am being treated with such contempt by this man."
Without making any announcement, he came straight up before Śāriputra and released a poisonous vapor, intending to cause him harm.
Śāriputra warded it off with his compassionate wisdom; his countenance became even more radiant and not a single hair on his body stirred.

He released poisonous vapors three times, yet none could cause him harm; thus he knew the Venerable One’s dignity, and his mind was liberated as wholesome thoughts arose. He then beheld Śāriputra seven times from above to below with a heart of loving-kindness.
Śāriputra then returned to the vihāra; at that moment, the person who had been swallowed by the python breathed its last and was about to pass away.
On that very day, heaven and earth shook violently; for while the most virtuous can cause heaven and earth to tremble, so too can the most wicked.
At that time, King Magadha went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself on the ground, and asked the World-Honored One:
"When a human *māhika* dies, to which realm will he go?
The Buddha said:
"In this life, he has been reborn in the first heaven.
When the king heard the Buddha’s words, he was astonished and questioned the Buddha further, saying:
"How can one who has committed such great sins be reborn in heaven?"
The Buddha said:

"Because Śāriputra looked up and down at her seven times with a mind of loving-kindness, by virtue of this merit he was born in the first heaven; when his merit is exhausted, he shall be born in the second heaven. After seven such cycles, he shall attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha and enter parinirvāṇa."
The king said to the Buddha,
"Will the seventy-two thousand people no longer have to repay their karmic debts?
The Buddha replied:

"In his final life as a Pratyekabuddha, his body shall be like purple-polished gold. At that time, he will be sitting beneath a tree by the side of a road. When he enters meditative absorption, a great army of more than seventy thousand men will pass by; seeing the Pratyekabuddha, they will think him to be a statue of gold. They will immediately seize it, cut it apart, and divide it among themselves. As soon as it falls into their hands, they will see it is but flesh. They will all gather it back together and depart. Thereupon, the Pratyekabuddha will enter Parinirvāṇa."
"The sins of this present life shall be fully expiated by such a meager recompense at that time.
The Buddha told the King:
"One who encounters a virtuous friend can have even mountain-like heaps of sin extinguished, and may likewise attain the Way."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the king and the great assembly were all filled with great joy; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.

(39) Once there was a śramaṇa sitting beneath a tree reciting the sūtras. A bird came and perched in the tree to listen to the recitation; it listened with single-minded concentration, neither looking left nor right, until it was shot and killed by a hunter.

When the bird was on the verge of death, its mind remained undisturbed; its spirit was immediately reborn in the heavens, where it reflected upon the source from which it had come and thus recognized its past life.
Having been reborn in heaven, they descended and scattered flowers over the śramaṇa beneath the tree.
The celestial being said to the practitioner,
"By virtue of the merit and blessings resulting from the favor of your recitation of the sūtras, O practitioner, I have escaped this avian body and attained the status of a celestial being."
Upon hearing the bird’s speech, the practitioner immediately attained the fruit of the Path; in an instant, he suddenly vanished, and the deva returned to his original abode.
The Master said:

“Those who study the Path and whose minds remain undisturbed at the time of death will not fall into the miserable realms of suffering upon rebirth. They will recognize their past lives and the places from which they have come; therefore, this sutra has been produced to show this to future generations!”
40. Once, when the Buddha was in the world, there was an elderly man seven *li* from the Jeta Grove who was fond of drinking alcohol. His disciple Ānanda went to him to exhort and advise him, saying:
"The Buddha is here now; you ought to go and see him."
The husband said:

"I have heard that the Buddha is here and I wish to go see him. The Buddha skillfully bestows the five precepts upon people, among which it is forbidden to drink alcohol. Just as a small child would die if deprived of milk, I cannot endure this; therefore, I will not go."

He again went out to drink wine; intoxicated by the wine, he returned to the road at dusk and stumbled over a tree stump, falling flat on the ground like a great mountain collapsing. His entire body was in agony, and he said to himself:
"How pleasant would this pain be!"
Ānanda often said to me,
"You should go to where the Buddha is.
I was unwilling to follow his words, and now my body is in pain beyond description.
He then said to the members of his household, both great and small:
"I wish to go to the place where the Buddha is.
Upon hearing this, everyone in the house was struck with astonishment.
"You previously refused to go to the Buddha's presence; for what reason do you wish to go now?
Having said this, he departed.
He stopped outside the gate of the Jeta Grove. At that time, Ānanda saw the old man approaching and joyfully addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A man from seven *li* away from the Jetavana has already arrived at the gate.
The Buddha said, "This old man could not have come alone; he must have come with the effort of five hundred white elephants!"
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “There were not five hundred elephants; he has come alone!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Five hundred white elephants are within your body.
Thereupon Ānanda called out to the man,
"Go forward and pay homage to the Buddha."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have long heard that the Buddha was here, yet due to my own folly, I did not come to pay my respects sooner; I pray that the Buddha will forgive my transgression!"
The Buddha asked the old man:
"If five hundred wagon-loads of firewood were piled on the ground and one wished to burn them all away, how many wagon-loads of fire would be required to burn them completely?"
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying, "There is no need for much fire; a fire the size of a bean will burn it away in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
The Buddha questioned the elder again:
"How long has it been since you put on these robes?
The Master replied,
"It has been one year since I put them on."
The Buddha asked the official again:
"If you wish to wash this garment to remove its impurities, how many years would it take to finish?
The official replied:
"One obtains one *dō* of pure lye; by washing for a brief moment, it becomes clean.
The Buddha said to the official:
"The accumulated sins of your honor are like five hundred cartloads of firewood, and also like the grime on a year's worth of clothing."
"The husband shall receive and uphold the five precepts from the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke several hundred words of a sutra; his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika*.

41 (Forty-one). Formerly, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Aśoka. He constructed a palace of great *kauśeya* silk, ten li in length and breadth, and summoned painters from all the small kingdoms. Upon their arrival, each painter painted various images according to his own inclination.

To the north of Kaśmīra there was a small kingdom that was the most distant; they sent a painter there, who arrived last. He observed that the walls and the surfaces of the roof were entirely covered with paintings, except for a space of five feet by the side of the doorway, which remained unpainted.
Again he looked up and observed the various objects, not knowing what they were; he thought to himself:

"When I first arrived, I passed by a small city. Beside the city was a pond with lotus flowers, and I saw a woman there, upright and beautiful, possessing the marks of one who could be a mother to the world."
Having reflected thus, he completed the painting of the city walls, the lotus pond, and the image of the woman.
Before the King had even entered the palace hall, he saw this painting and asked,
"Who painted this?"
He replied,
"The painter who arrived later.
He then asked:
"Do you see that it is made of form,
or is it made of emptiness?
He replied:
"It is not false that one acts upon seeing.
The King asked,
"Do you act in accordance with the form?"
"Is it for the sake of making them beautiful?
He replied, "It is not for the sake of making them beautiful; it is merely to conform to their natural forms!"
Realizing then that this woman was the mother of the world, he immediately dispatched a messenger to seek her hand in marriage for the position of Queen.
Having received his orders, the messenger went straight to her kingdom and, upon meeting the girl’s parents, said to them:
"The King seeks a virtuous woman to be his Queen."
The girl’s father said,
“How should we proceed regarding her marriage?
He then went to the girl’s husband’s house and spoke to him:
"The King has sent me to seek this maiden.
After traveling for three years, he arrived and said:
"Your Majesty has already taken her as the Most Honored One; you ought not to be stingy with her, so give her to the King at once."

"This husband is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who reflects that others might endanger his life for the sake of wealth or beauty; thinking that if he does not give her, they might even punish him, he then gave his wife to the messenger."

She returned and went to inform the King; upon seeing her, the King was greatly delighted and immediately appointed her as Queen. When she obtained beautiful flowers, she wept bitterly, and the King asked, "For what reason do you weep?"
The queen said,
"I shall speak only if Your Majesty pardons my offense.
The king said:
"Tell me why," the queen said.
"It is because this truly resembles my former husband, Xiang, that I weep!"
The king said in anger:
"You are the mother of the world, yet you still think of poverty and lowliness?
You are an old woman who ought to be punished."

The King then dispatched a messenger to investigate the matter of his former husband, intending to determine whether he possessed the fragrance or not; if he did not possess it, he was to be punished.
The messenger went to inquire of the man’s family, and they said:
"After this worthy man lost his wife, he informed his parents and departed to become a śramaṇa, whereupon he attained the path of Arhatship."
The messenger went to the Buddha’s kingdom and said,
"The King wishes to see and make offerings to the practitioner.
The practitioner replied:
"I myself do not exist; furthermore, what is there to see as 'me'?
The messenger replied, "The King wishes to make offerings to the practitioner."
The practitioner followed the messenger and went to inform the king. When the king saw the practitioner, the fragrance of his body was even more intense than that of a lotus flower.
The king said, "This man has smeared his body with incense."
He simply bathed him in hot water, and the fragrance became even more intense; he then wrapped his body in fine silk, and the fragrance of his body doubled again.
The king then believed him and asked:
"By what cause and condition has the practitioner attained such fragrance? I pray you, instruct me."
The practitioner said to the king:

"In a previous life, I was a Brahmin. While traveling, I saw someone preaching the sutras; with palms joined and a joyful heart, I single-mindedly praised the Bodhisattva and offered a small amount of incense as an act of worship. Consequently, I attained merit that led me to the fruit of the Way."

42 (42). Once there were a father and son living together who entered the mountains to clear a forest. There was gold in a spring, and the son returned home to seek his portion from his father, saying:
"I do not need anything else; let all my possessions go to you, father, but give me only one set of ox-cart and oxen, two *sheng* of rice, and one each of a reed-cutter and an axe."
The father would not listen to him.
Although he admonished him repeatedly without ceasing, the father finally gave him his consent, saying:
"Do not come back to me again!"
The son then entered the mountains to dig for gold in a spring, but day after day he was unable to obtain any.

The father went with him to look; observing such gold, he looked up at the edge of the mountain peak and saw gold as vast as a mountain reflected in the water. He then climbed the mountain and brought down the gold to the ground using a large wooden pole.
The father said to his son:
"How should one seek it according to the Dharma?
Simply by digging for water, when will it ever be obtained?"
"The son does not understand those who seek gold: if a person does not uphold the five precepts but merely pursues sounds and forms, how can they ever regain a human body!

The father is like the wise man seeking gold; when he contemplates the beginning and end of things, he upholds the Buddha’s five precepts and practices the ten wholesome actions to be reborn in heaven. Thus, his human body is never lost from lifetime to lifetime, and he shall later attain the fruit of the Buddha-way.
43 (Forty-three). Formerly, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was on intimate terms with the seventh Brahmā.
At that time, Brahmā descended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to sport together [with Śakra], but Śakra was sorrowful and unhappy. Brahmā asked Śakra:
"Why are you unhappy?"
The commentary states:
"Do you see how rare it is for those from the heavens to be reborn as humans?

Those from the lower realms no longer perform wholesome deeds; they all enter the evil paths and none are born above again. When celestial beings descend to be born among humans, they rarely return [to their heavenly state] once more; this is why I am sorrowful!"
Brahmā said to Śakra:

"You shall die and transform yourself into a lion of extreme majesty and power; I shall transform myself into a brāhmaṇa. Together we will descend to Jambudvīpa to instruct the world in doing good, so that those who do good, upon dying, shall all be reborn in heaven."
Thereupon, each followed their respective transformation and descended to a certain country.
Within the city gate, Siṃha said:
"I wish to be eaten by humans."
When the people of the country saw this, there was none who was not struck with terror; they prostrated themselves, begging for mercy, yet he still refused to depart.
The transformed Brahmin spoke to the people, saying:
"This lion is fierce; it shall depart of its own accord once it has received thirty men who are condemned to death."
The king then sent thirty prisoners who were destined for death to the lion. Once the lion had received the men, he drove them away into the deep mountains.
Before he could devour them, a transformed deity spoke to the people:
"If you can uphold the five precepts, mindfully practice the ten paths of wholesome action, and ensure that your body, speech, and mind are in accord, this lion will not devour you."
The people said, "We are about to die; what does this matter? We can certainly bear it.
They then received the precepts from the transformed person, and the lion no longer devoured them.
The lion said, "Let him go;
however, I know your heart. If you do not uphold the five precepts of the Buddha, I shall surely devour you."
When those thirty men returned to their country, the people were all astonished upon seeing them and asked,
"How have you managed to return?
They replied:
“There was a man who taught us to receive the Buddha’s five precepts; because of this, the lion no longer devours us, and so we have come here to take refuge!
The lion then stayed at the city gate, and the people of the kingdom were greatly terrified; they all received the five precepts from the thirty men.

The Lion then departed and traveled to another kingdom; in this manner, he traversed all eighty thousand kingdoms, causing everyone to practice virtue. Those who died were reborn in the heavens, where there was even greater joy, abundance, and prosperity, and the realms were filled with many beings.
The Bodhisattva’s skillful means for delivering sentient beings were thus, until he himself attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The one who transformed into a lion as Śakra was my own self; the one who transformed into a Brahmin as Brahmā is now Kāśyapa.”
"At that time, you assisted me in transforming and delivering the people of the world, enabling me to attain Buddhahood; therefore, I sit beside you now to repay the kindness of that time.
(44) Formerly, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a king named Kuśinī who established a vihāra for the Buddha and fulfilled all its requirements.
The seventh daughter of the king had previously served a brahmin, but later came to believe in and serve the Buddha; the brahmin detested her and gave her the name "Monk's Slave.
The king had ten strange dreams and questioned them.
The brahmin, intending to harm the girl through a dream, said to the king:
"It is auspicious only if you obtain your most beloved daughter and burn her as an offering to the gods.
The king was deeply distressed.
The woman asked the king,
"Why are you not joyful?
When the king had explained it thus, the woman said:
“I shall take responsibility for the portion of the *śārgaka* sacrifice!
He asked, “On what day shall the sacrifice be performed?”
The brahmin said,
"Seven days from now.
The daughter addressed the king:
"Though I am facing death, I pray that you permit me to go to the Buddha’s dwelling, so that all the people south of the city may escort me out.
He then gave the order for her to be sent away.
The woman was led to the Buddha’s presence; he preached the Dharma to her, and she fully realized the Truth.
On the first day, those from one side of the city all attained the vision of the Truth.
On the second day, he sought out those within the city to send them, and it was likewise.
For six days, he sought the King and the officials of the palace to send them forth.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all realized the Truth.
The King then realized that the Brahmin had deceived him and said to him:
"You nearly caused my daughter's death; if you do not become a śramaṇa under the Buddha, you must leave this country."
The brahmin, not knowing where he had gone, had no choice but to go to the Buddha and become a śramaṇa; later, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
*Za piyu jing* (Sanskrit: *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*), Scroll Lower.
